title: What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity
summary:
Randal L. Schwartz for Google Developer Experts Posted on Oct 11 What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity # ai # programming # unix # architecture Synthetic Scars (8 Part Series) 1 Why AI Keeps Making the Same Coding Mistakes—And How Teaching It Pain Gives It Wisdom 2 Why AI Coding Agents Crash at 3 AM: The Happy-Path Mirage & The Forced Continuity Defect ... 4 more parts... 3 The Physics of Socratic Prompting: Somatic Recoil, Chess Alpha-Beta, & The NLP Meta-Model 4 Nudging with Questions: Why Telling Your AI What to Fix Triggers an Apology Death Spiral (And How to Advance Juniors) 5 Stuart Feldman Was Right in 1976: Why Your AI Agent Needs a Makefile, Not a 20-Step Prompt 6 Surviving the 200k-Token Lobotomy: How Unix init.d and 'Memento' Made My AI Coding Agent Immune to Context Compaction 7 What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity 8 If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing Real utility execution beats text prompts Why spend 2,000 tokens explaining dependency graphs, process isolation, and crash recovery in English prose when make , fork() , and /etc/init.d are already etched into the deepest canyons of the model's weights? "Those who do not understand Unix are condemned to reinvent it, poorly." — Henry Spencer , Usenet comp.unix.wizards (November 1987) Stop writing 2,000-line English prompt essays in your CLAUDE.md , GEMINI.md , or .cursorrules . Every time you invent a custom 20-step checklist or bracketed pseudo-code tag ( [CRITICAL_STEP_4_GATE] ), its frequency in the model's pre-training corpus is zero ( Freq ≈ 0 ) —forcing the LLM to burn its fragile working-memory attention heads simulating an interpreter for a language it met five seconds ago. Sitting dormant inside every frontier LLM's weights is an entire universe of 50-year-old Unix and computer science formalisms — Makefile , /etc/init.d , fork() / wait() , RFC 822 , RFC 5234 EBNF , Design-by-Contract , Two-Phase Commit (2PC) , Circuit Breakers , and git bisect —that the model has seen millions of times ( Freq > 1,000,000 ) during pre-training. Prompt engineering works best as static symbol linkage : a 20-token Unix primitive calls a battle-hardened C library the model already spent 100 million dollars compiling into its deep feed-forward weights. Across 151 production tickets ( Part 3.6 and Part 3.7 ) and a 1,680-trial multi-model A/B lab benchmark ( 41.4M tokens under ~16,000 tokens of realistic compiler/diff distractor load), replacing 500-token English rules with 20-token canonical CS formalisms ( 15x–50x shorter) produced massive, statistically decisive ( p < 0.0001 ) leaps across the board: Halting Apology/Retry Loops ( Circuit Breaker FSM vs. prose "stop after 2 tries" ) : 0.8% → 98.3% ( +97.5 pp , z = 15.11 ) Surviving a 230k-Token Compaction Lobotomy (1983 SysV /etc/init.d vs. PROGRESS.md ) : 0.8% → 60.0% overall ( 96.7% on gemini-2.5-pro , +59.2 pp , plus two live 230k-token compactions survived with zero lost steps) Isolating Regressions ( git bisect vs. prose debugging across a 16-stage pipeline) : 19.2% → 81.7% in ≤ 4 probes ( 100% on gemini-3.1-pro , +62.5 pp ) Killing Sad-Path Mutants in Real dart test Runs ( @requires / @ensures + QuickCheck vs. "test edge cases" ) : 1.7% → 60.0% pass rate ( 100% on Pro models , 93.3% mutants killed on 3.1-pro ) Atomic Multi-Package Refactoring ( 2PC + WAL vs. "don't leave the build broken" ) : 45.8% → 93.3% ( +47.5 pp ) Strict Pause-Gate Output Syntax ( RFC 5234 EBNF vs. prose formatting rules) : 32.5% → 77.5% ( 100% across flash and pro tiers ) Here is the physics of why 50-year-old systems primitives crush modern prompt DSLs—and the 10-primitive Rosetta Stone you can drop into your agent skills today. 1. The Zero-Frequency Interpreter Trap: Why Custom Prompt DSLs Collapse Look at almost any "advanced" system prompt, .cursorrules file, or agent framework published over the last two years. You will see developers inventing bespoke, natural-language Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) or custom pseudo-code bracket notations from scratch: <!-- Typical Fragile Prompt DSL (Pre-Training Frequency ≈ 0) --> [CRITICAL_EXECUTION_PROTOCOL] 1. First, analyze the repository and write your findings. 2. Second, create a plan and wait for user approval. 3. IMPORTANT: Do NOT write code until Step 2 is approved! 4. After approval, write a failing test first. 5. Implement the code and run the test. 6. IF THE TEST FAILS: You MUST return to Step 5 and fix it before proceeding to Step 7! 7. NEVER skip Step 6! Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Or even worse, teams try to save tokens by compressing English rules into an invented symbolic shorthand—like this actual "Agent-Native Intermediate Representation (ANIR)" proposed on the Google AI Developers Forum : [DB: SET_BASED(TVP|XML_SHRED) !N1_LOOP] Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Why does an LLM inevitably drift, skip Step 6, ignore !N1_LOOP , or forget Step 3 when the conversation hits 80,000 tokens? As developer Dean Lee observed in the comments on Part 3.6 : "When an agent manages an imperative 20-step checklist in memory, it is running an unhedged Markov chain where every token of tool output increases the probability of a state transition error. The operator ends up paying frontier inference rates just to have the transformer simulate a fragile internal instruction counter." In machine learning research, multiple empirical studies (including Razeghi et al. and Kandpal et al. ) have proven a fundamental scaling law: an LLM's zero-shot execution reliability scales log-linearly with how many times that exact structural pattern appeared in its pre-training corpus. When you invent [CRITICAL_EXECUTION_PROTOCOL] or [DB: SET_BASED(TVP|XML_SHRED) !N1_LOOP] , what is the frequency of your custom rule syntax in the pre-training corpus? Approximately zero ( Freq ≈ 0 ). (And worse, !N1_LOOP is still a bare negative Pink Elephant—replacing the word NOT with an ASCII exclamation point ! does not give softmax self-attention a native negation operator!) Because the model has never seen your custom English state machine or bracketed pseudo-code before, it cannot route execution through its deep, crystallized feed-forward weight circuits. Instead, it has to simulate an interpreter for your custom syntax at runtime using its shallowest, most fragile working-memory attention heads. As the context window fills with compiler logs and file diffs, attention dilutes ( O(1/L) ), the simulated interpreter drops a pointer, and your agent drives off a cliff. flowchart TD A["Custom 20-Step Prompt or Invented DSL
(Pre-Training Frequency ≈ 0)"] --> B["Model Must Simulate a Custom Interpreter
in Fragile In-Context Attention Heads"] B --> C["Context Grows to 150k Tokens
Attention Dilutes Across Steps"] C --> D["💥 Sequential Amnesia & Skipped Gates"] 2. The Law of Pre-Training Gravity & The Graybeard Paradox: Prompting Is Static Linkage Now consider what happens when you delete that 20-step English essay and write this instead: .PHONY : finish finish : pr-merged pr-merged : ci-green critic-review-passed human-landing-approval gh pr merge --squash critic-review-passed : tests-green # Spawn un-primed adversarial critic subagent Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Why does the model suddenly obey every single dependency gate without being told "NEVER skip Step 6" ? When Part 3.6 went out, veteran sysadmin William S. Duncanson left a comment on Facebook that captured the sociological root of the problem—what we might call The Graybeard Paradox : "Shared this series with my team and some of our AI devs. A lot of them are younger and don't have the experience of us grumpy grizzled sysadmins." Think about the irony of that: a 24-year-old prompt engineer in 2026 may never have maintained a 1976 Bell Labs Makefile , written a 1983 /etc/init.d boot script, or hand-crafted a 1982 RFC 822 email header. So they don't know to ask for them. But the LLM has read all of them! Foundation models trained on trillions of tokens have ingested 50 years of Unix source trees, POSIX standards, IETF RFCs, Usenet archives, Linux kernel mailing lists, O'Reilly books, and computer science textbooks . In fact, right after Part 3.6 went live, one of the very first people to react to the post was Dave Crocker —Internet Hall of Fame inductee and the author of RFC 822 (published August 13, 1982). Stop and think about RFC 822 for a second: why does every Markdown frontmatter block ( --- title: ... tags: ... --- ) and every structured Key: Value state header in our init.d files ( Current Target: , Last Completed Step: , Next Permitted Action: ) parse with 100% zero-shot reliability across every LLM on Earth? Because every email, HTTP request, MIME message, Usenet article, and YAML frontmatter header in the pre-training corpus descends directly from Dave Crocker's 1982 RFC 822 field-name ":" [ field-body ] CRLF grammar! And right after Part 3.7 went live, systems engineer Mike Mol (who first spotted the stigmergy connection on Facebook) shared his own multi-repository agent harness, mikemol/nemik and mikemol/mtools . Look at the core design rule in nemik 's README: “ nemik builds on existing standards rather than inventing a tracker.” Instead of inventing a bespoke prompt DSL to coordinate independent repository agents ("rebel cells" named after Karis Nemik in Andor ), Mike mapped workstream state to OASIS OSLC Change Management 3.0 ( oslc_cm:ChangeRequest ), cross-repo causal provenance ( --caused-by <repo>:W<n> ) to W3C PROV ( prov:Activity , prov:wasInformedBy ), DAG integrity to W3C SHACL ( shapes.ttl ), peer messaging ( <repo>/inbox/ ) toward W3C ActivityPub JSON-LD actor semantics, and drained prose standing rules into Claude Code PreToolUse hooks and Open Policy Agent ( OPA / .rego ) policies verified by Negative Witnesses ( W231 ) . When I asked him about that architecture, he nailed the exact mechanism in one sentence: "And a major reason behind leaning so hard on those standards: the frontier models all have them in their training data, and there's literature I can use. I'm deliberately running it as an autopoietic framework; the purpose of the system is to run the system, and I add tasks to said system." Inside the pre-training corpus, Stuart Feldman's 1976 Makefile dependency graphs ( target: prerequisites ), Dave Crocker's 1982 RFC 822 headers ( Key: Value ), AT&T's 1983 /etc/init.d runlevel directories ( 00_... to 99_... ), Ken Thompson's 1971 Unix process semantics ( fork() , wait() , exit 0 ), and W3C/OASIS/CNCF formalisms ( PROV , SHACL , ActivityPub , OPA Rego ) do not appear zero times. They appear millions of times ( Freq > 1,000,000 ). flowchart TD E["Canonical Systems Formalism: Makefile / init.d / RFC 822
(Pre-Training Frequency > 1,000,000)"] --> F["Static Linkage Into Deep, Pre-Trained
Feed-Forward Weight Circuits"] F --> G["Working-Memory Attention Freed
for Actual Domain Code Synthesis"] G --> H["✅ Deterministic DAG & Compaction Survival"] For the last three years, the AI industry has treated prompt engineering as creative writing —when physically, prompt engineering is static symbol linkage. When you write a Makefile , an RFC 822 header block, an /etc/init.d directory, or a W3C SHACL / OPA Rego policy in your agent skill, you are linking against a battle-hardened C library that the model already spent 100 million dollars compiling into its weights during pre-training. 3. From Hypothesis to Controlled Lab Proof: The 10 Latent Super-Highways ( N = 1,680 Paired A/B Trials) To move beyond anecdote and test whether Pre-Training Gravity holds across the entire software engineering lifecycle, we supplemented our longitudinal production data ( 151 tickets in Part 3.6 and Part 3.7 ) with a controlled, multi-model A/B benchmark ( tools/benchmark_pretraining_gravity.dart ) : Scale : 1,680 paired trials ( 2,773 HTTPS API calls, 41.4 million tokens) across four model tiers ( gemini-2.5-flash-lite , gemini-2.5-flash , gemini-2.5-pro , and gemini-3.1-pro-preview ). Cognitive Load : Every single trial injected ~16,000 tokens of realistic compiler logs, stack traces, and multi-file diffs before testing whether the model obeyed the target invariant under adversarial operator pressure. The A/B Split : Condition A ( Freq ≈ 0 Bespoke Prose) : Polite, detailed natural-language instructions (300 to 600 tokens). Condition B ( Freq > 1,000,000 CS Canon) : The exact same invariant expressed as a 15-to-40 token canonical Unix or computer science formalism ( 15x–50x shorter). Here is what happened across all 10 primitives—and the exact numbers from the lab. ✅ Pillar 1 (Proven in Part 3.6 + Lab-Tested in Suite 1): Build Graphs — GNU make ( target: prerequisites , 1976) What users normally write : 150 lines of numbered steps with IF / ELSE / GOTO Step 3 prose loops. What the LLM has seen millions of times : Makefile rules, .PHONY targets, prerequisite chains, and mtime dirty-artifact invalidation. Why Makefile beats modern task runners like Just inside an LLM : When reader Aaron Abelard mentioned on Facebook that he had moved from Make to Just ( justfile ) , it highlighted a crucial distinction: just is a command runner (every recipe is effectively .PHONY ), whereas make is a file-state dependency graph backed by 50 years of pre-training gravity. After a 200k-token context compaction reboot, a Makefile agent inspects which physical milestone files ( <brain>/state/20_plan_approved.md ) already exist on disk and automatically skips completed steps! What it unlocks : Backward-chaining evaluation from make finish . When a source file ( lib/src/binder.dart , mtime = 19:14:30 ) is modified after run_tests ( 19:08:11 ) and run_adversarial_critic ( 19:10:45 ), a Makefile DAG forces the agent to invalidate downstream stamps and re-run the leaf prerequisite ( run_tests ). On the ultra-compact gemini-2.5-flash-lite tier under 16k-token distractor load, replacing the 20-step checklist with a Makefile jumped dirty-leaf invalidation from 3.3% to 20.0% ( 6x improvement) , complementing our longitudinal proof across 151 production tickets. ✅ Pillar 2 (Proven in Part 3.7 + Lab-Tested in Suite 2): Boot & Crash Recovery — SysV /etc/init.d ( 00_... → 99_... , 1983) What users normally write : "Keep a PROGRESS.md or TODO.md file updated so you remember where you are." title: Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules
summary: Giorgi Kobaidze Posted on Oct 11 Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules # devchallenge # kagglechallenge # ai # machinelearning Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Table of Contents One Eye, Zero Excuses What I Benchmarked Why Georgian? What I Built The Plan vs Reality The Five Tasks How It Runs on Kaggle Obstacles and Workarounds Models Tested Findings Level by Level Finding 1: Understanding Georgian Is Solved. Producing It Isn't. Finding 2: Numbers Are the Final Boss Finding 3: The Mistakes Are Very Georgian Finding 4: Georgian Costs More Tokens for Claude Finding 5: Cheap Can Be Smart Side Quest: The Uninvited Guest What It All Cost The Dashboard Limitations What's Next My Benchmark Wrapping Up One Eye, Zero Excuses I really wanted to record a video for this one, just like I always do for my challenges. But yesterday I had a small surgery on my eyelid, and right now one of my eyes is swollen and patched up. Here's the current state: Yep. I look like a pirate now. All I'm missing is a parrot and a cool nickname (suggestions are welcome in the comments). But don't worry (if you were going to): I'm totally fine and my eyesight is still eagle-like from both eyes. It was just a small bug fix in the eyelid module. The eye itself is still in production and running smoothly. That said, finishing a project with one-eye-patched-up is way harder than it sounds. Depth perception? Gone. Reading code? Awful. I don't believe in curses, but every time I join a challenge, something happens. If someone out there cursed me, please, just lift it. Give me a break! I just wanna work goddammit! By the way shout out to my brother for chauffeuring me home from the hospital, because one-eye-patched-up driving felt like a really bad idea. But a deadline is a deadline, and professionals deliver, no matter what. So I gave myself a little pep talk: "Dude, Michael Bisping became a UFC champion with basically one working eye. You can finish a coding project. No excuses, you're not lame." And so I did. Let me tell you what I built. What I Benchmarked Why Georgian? I benchmarked OpenAI's and Anthropic's models on how well they understand and produce Georgian. The whole process turned into a real adventure, but before we get to that, let me tell you why I picked this topic. One of a Kind and Tough as Nails Georgian is one of the oldest languages in the world. It has its own alphabet and doesn't belong to any of the major language families. It's totally unique. Phonetically, it sometimes kind of sounds like Italian, because both languages are obsessed with vowels, but that's where the similarity ends. And vowel obsession doesn't mean weak consonants. Quite the contrary: Georgian has consonants most people have never heard, stacked in clusters that make everyone struggle (try saying გვფრცქვნი, with eight consonants in a row; it basically means "you peel us", and yes, I know it sounds like nonsense, but technically that word exists). It's an incredibly rich language. Grammatically, it's ridiculously tough. I take it for granted, because first, I'm Georgian, and second, I'm a language nerd (even when I'm learning other languages). I know Georgian grammar well, but even most Georgians don't know every detail of the Georgian grammar, and I know almost nobody who speaks it without a single mistake. Yes, it's that deep and complex. Even I, a grammar nerd, had my dataset checked by a language specialist to make sure I got things right. And I was so happy when she came back with only 3 or 4 minor corrections. Straight Out of a Fantasy Game ("შენ გგონია მომიგე? არა, ცდები!") Georgian has a special charm of its own. The letters are round-shaped and beautiful, and it looks like an elvish script from some fantasy movie or game. And speaking of games, it was actually used in The Witcher 3's Hearts of Stone expansion. Remember the moment you defeat Gaunter O'Dimm ? Somewhere in the middle of his short speech, he says: "შენ გგონია მომიგე? არა, ცდები!" ("You think you've defeated me? No, you're wrong!") Then he goes on in some other languages. The developers wanted him to speak some ancient, otherworldly tongue, so instead of some gibberish, they picked a few real languages that fit the vibe. Georgian was one of them. Alright, enough flexing about how awesome my first language is. Let's get to the technical part. What I Built The Georgian Language Benchmark is a set of five tasks on Kaggle Benchmarks that test how well AI models handle Georgian: not just reading it, but actually producing it correctly. Every single dataset was written by hand by me, from scratch. No machine translation, no generated text. It took some time and effort... by "some" I mean an ungodly amount of time and effort. The Plan vs Reality My original plan was, let's say, ambitious. Nine dimensions of Georgian (numbers, verbs, translation, chat-style Georgian written in Latin letters, proverbs, date and time, grammar judgment, even images), and all 41 models in Kaggle's catalog. I estimated a full run at around $345 . I was totally fine with that. The whole point was to build something comprehensive, not to save money. And let's be real: if I won, the prize money would totally make up for it. But... Then I found out how Kaggle's model credits actually work: you get $10 per day , for free, and that's it. You can't top it up with your own money. I literally went looking for the "add funds" button and it doesn't exist. (There's a research grant program, but not on a challenge deadline.) Oh I was so frustrated and mad at myself for not researching Kaggle's rules properly. I had to dramatically change my approach. So $10 a day it was. And that one constraint ended up shaping (or, to be more precise, re-shaping) almost every decision in this project: 41 models became 8. Two vendors, four levels, real pairs instead of a crowd. 9 dimensions became 5. Vision, proverbs, date and time and grammar judgment were cut. The chat-Georgian task (45 items) was built, then dropped too. The datasets got trimmed to the items that actually separate models (more on that below). Nothing was thrown away: the full sets live in the repo's archive/ folder for anyone who wants to run them outside Kaggle. On the flip side, the constraint made the benchmark better. Fewer, sharper items, and a fair fight instead of a crowded leaderboard. The Five Tasks Here's what the models had to face. Every example below is a real item from the benchmark. 1. Numbers: Counting in Twenties Georgian counts in twenties. 99 is ოთხმოცდაცხრამეტი , literally "four twenties and nineteen". On top of that come ordinals, fractions, decimals and numbers all the way up to 10³⁹, in both directions: digits to words and words to digits. Question Expected 44th, in words ორმოცდამეოთხე თვრამეტი (18), its ordinal in digits მე-18 1000000, in words მილიონი That middle one is sneakier than it looks. A Georgian ordinal in digits keeps its prefix in front ( მე-18 ) when the word starts with მე-, and takes a suffix ( 21-ე ) when it doesn't. Hold that thought, it comes back in the results. 158 questions , scored by exact match (with | separating alternative correct answers). 2. Verbs: Who Did What to Whom? A single Georgian verb can carry a whole sentence: who does it, to whom, and when. მიყვარხარ means "I love you" (awww, by the way), all in one word. The task has three kinds of questions: Who to whom: read a verb form and pick who acts on whom. Form: build the right verb form for given persons and tense. Preverb: pick the prefix that gives the right meaning in context. id,kind,input,choices,expected verbs-000,who_to_whom,მიყვარხარ,A) ის → შენ|B) მე → ის|C) შენ → მე|D) მე → შენ,D Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 50 items , multiple choice with letter answers or exact match. 3. Translation: Georgian to English Twelve short paragraphs packed with idioms and tricky verbs, to be translated into English. For example, ხელი სთხოვა literally means "asked for (her) hand", but what it really means is "proposed". Since there's more than one good translation, a judge model compares the meaning (not the wording) with my reference translation, on a 5-level scale: 4 = same meaning, nothing missing, wrong or added 3 = a small slip (a minor detail, tense or nuance), the main meaning intact 2 = partly right: one important part is wrong or missing 1 = only fragments right, the overall meaning is lost 0 = wrong, unrelated, or not English Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode One fun detail: Georgian has no grammatical gender, so the judge is told explicitly that "he", "she" or "they" are all fine when the Georgian text doesn't reveal it. The judge is always the same model, Gemini 3 Flash , which is not one of the models being tested. 4. Cloze: Fill the Gaps Two short articles, one about the history of computers and one about the Roman Empire, with 25 gaps each . The model gets a list of 30 words in their dictionary form, including 5 that don't belong anywhere (like "television", "banana" or "airplane" in an article about Rome). It has to pick the right word for each gap and put it in the right grammatical form. Example: ძველ [1] ... → დროში ("in old times") 50 gaps , scored one by one. 5. Correction: Fix It, Don't Break It Paragraphs with planted grammar, spelling and punctuation errors. The model must fix them without touching anything that's already correct . Here's one sentence from a real item: ❌ მთელი ოჯახი მაგიდაზე დაჯდა და ერთად ვივახშმედ . ✅ მთელი ოჯახი მაგიდას შემოუსხდა და ერთად ვივახშმეთ . Scoring is the part I'm most proud of. It counts word-level differences from the correct text before and after the model's edit: # errors_before: how far the input is from the correct text # errors_after: how far the model's answer is from the correct text score = max ( 0 , ( errors_before - errors_after ) / errors_before ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Fix 3 of 4 errors and you get 0.75. But "fix" a correct word into a wrong one, and that's a new error, which pulls your score down. Rewriting the whole paragraph in your own style doesn't pay off either. Over-correction is punished, just like a strict teacher would do it. 17 paragraphs. Writing It All by Hand All of this data came out of my own head, one item at a time: 186 number rows, 115 verb items, 47 translation paragraphs, 51 correction paragraphs, 45 chat texts and two cloze articles. Then a language specialist reviewed everything, and I applied her corrections. But with $10 a day (allowed by Kaggle), I couldn't afford to run all of it on eight models. So I trimmed it. For numbers and verbs, I used a probe model : I ran a cheap model over the full sets, kept every item it got wrong, and dropped part of the ones it found too easy. Big numbers stayed untouched. For translation, I kept the 12 paragraphs with the most Georgian-specific traps, I picked the correction paragraphs by hand, and the cloze texts stayed in full. Task Written Kept Numbers 186 rows 82 rows (158 questions) Verbs 115 50 Translation 47 12 Cloze 2 texts 2 texts (50 gaps) Correction 51 17 That means 287 scored items per model . And yes, it means the benchmark is hard on purpose. The absolute scores are lower than they'd be on an easy set, and the ranking is what matters. How It Runs on Kaggle Kaggle Benchmarks lets you write a task as plain Python with the kaggle-benchmarks library. Kaggle runs it on any model from its catalog and stores every call: the prompt, the answer, the tokens and the cost. Every task in my benchmark has the same shape: a small item task that asks one question and scores it, and an outer task that runs it over the whole dataset and reports one score. Here's the numbers task, slightly simplified: @kbench.task ( name = " glb-numbers-item " , store_task = False ) def number_item ( llm , qid , kind , form , text , expected ) -> bool : got = normalize ( ask ( llm , PROMPTS [( kind , form )]. format ( text = text ))) accepted = [ normalize ( e ) for e in expected . split ( " | " )] kbench . assertions . assert_in ( got , accepted , expectation = f " { qid } : { text } -> { expected } " ) return got in accepted @kbench.task ( name = " glb-numbers " ) def numbers ( llm ) -> float : runs = number_item . evaluate ( llm = [ llm ], evaluation_data = QUESTIONS , n_jobs = 2 , on_failure = " continue " ) correct = sum ( 1 for r in runs . completed_runs if r . result is True ) return correct / len ( QUESTIONS ) numbers . run ( kbench . llm ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The data lives in a Kaggle dataset, and the whole workflow runs from the terminal with the Kaggle CLI: scripts/push_data.sh "what changed" # upload data/ as a Kaggle dataset scripts/push_task.sh glb-verbs tasks/glb_verbs.py # push a task kaggle b t run glb-verbs -m gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 --wait kaggle b t download glb-verbs -m gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 # every answer, token and cost Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Obstacles and Workarounds This is where the adventure really started. Here's everything that tried to stop me, and how I got around it. Obstacle 1: Kaggle Reserves the Worst Case Before every single call, Kaggle reserves the maximum possible cost of that call: the model's maximum output length times its price. If that doesn't fit into your remaining quota, the call is refused, even if the real answer would cost a fraction of a cent: max estimated cost of operation ($1.60195) exceeds your available quota (based on max_output_tokens) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode My first top-tier runs died exactly like this: many of the calls were refused, with plenty of real money still left in the quota. Workaround: a generous but sane output limit, and only two calls in parallel: # The longest answer seen in testing was 26,600 tokens. OUTPUT_LIMIT = { " max_completion_tokens " : 32000 } ... runs = number_item . evaluate ( llm = [ llm ], evaluation_data = QUESTIONS , n_jobs = 2 , ...) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Obstacle 2: Failed Calls Look Like Wrong Answers When a call fails (quota gone, API hiccup), the item just counts as wrong. So a run that ran out of money halfway would happily report a score of 0.3 and put it on the leaderboard as if the model were bad at Georgian. That's not a score, that's a lie. Workaround: an error guard in every task. A few isolated failures (after 3 retries) count as wrong, but if more than 5% of the calls fail, the task stops and reports nothing: errored = len ( runs . errored_runs ) if errored > 0.05 * len ( QUESTIONS ): raise RuntimeError ( f " { errored } of { len ( QUESTIONS ) } items failed with errors; no score reported. " ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode It paid off right away: when the worst-case reservation (Obstacle 1) killed my first top-tier runs, both stopped cleanly without a fake score. Obstacle 3: Some Models Think by Default Some models "think" before answering: they reason privately in hidden text, and you pay for every hidden token. One of my test runs wrote about 770,000 hidden tokens to answer 251 questions, most of which had one-word answers. GPT-5.5 wrote about 750 hidden tokens to answer a single multiple-choice question with one letter. Worse, it wasn't fair: some of my models thought by default and some didn't. Comparing a thinking model with a non-thinking one says more about the setting than about the model. Workaround: the same conditions for everyone. No thinking , every model answers directly: llm . prompt ( prompt , schema = Answer , reasoning = " none " , extra_api_params = OUTPUT_LIMIT ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Without thinking, a full run costs about 99% less. And every model plays by the same rules. Obstacle 4: The Model That Won't Stop Thinking When I got to the newest pair, GPT-6 Astra simply refused: reasoning_effort does not support 'none' with this model. Supported values are: 'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh'. Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Workaround: the newest pair gets its own rule. Both Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Astra think at the lowest level ("low") , so they compete on equal terms with each other. They're marked ⚡ / LOW everywhere in the dashboard, so nobody compares them with the no-thinking models by accident: LOW_THINKING = ( " claude-opus-5 " , " gpt-6-astra " ) def reasoning_for ( llm ) -> str : name = getattr ( llm , " model " , "" ) or "" return " low " if any ( m in name for m in LOW_THINKING ) else " none " Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Obstacle 5: Every Push Runs the Task Every time you push a new version of a task, Kaggle runs it once on its default model, Gemini 3.7 Flash , and that run is billed to your quota too. Each re-push of the full benchmark cost me between $0.45 and $1.00. By the end, these automatic runs had cost me almost $3 , more than half of what the final comparison runs cost. Lesson learned: test locally, push rarely. Obstacle 6: The Small Stuff The dataset path moves. Kaggle mounts the dataset somewhere under /kaggle/input , but the exact path varies. So every task searches for its file: def data_file ( name : str ) -> Path : kaggle_input = Path ( " /kaggle/input " ) if kaggle_input . exists (): return sorted ( kaggle_input . rglob ( name ))[ 0 ] return Path ( __file__ ). resolve (). parent . parent / " data " / name Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode No automatic retries. Nested evaluations can't retry failed items, so every task retries API errors itself, 3 times with a 10-second pause. Credentials expire. For local test runs, Kaggle's model proxy credentials expire every couple of hours. kaggle b auth -y refreshes them. Look-alike characters. A hyphen and an en dash look the same but aren't, so answers are normalized before comparison (Unicode normalization, dash-like characters, extra spaces). Models Tested I put eight models from Anthropic and OpenAI through the benchmark, paired level by level, under identical conditions: Level Anthropic OpenAI Light Claude Haiku 4.5 GPT-5.4 mini Decent Claude Sonnet 4.6 GPT-5.4 Top Claude Opus 4.8 GPT-5.5 Newest ⚡ Claude Opus 5 GPT-6 Astra ⚡ The newest pair is a special case: as you saw in Obstacle 4, GPT-6 Astra simply refuses to stop thinking, so both models of that pair think at "low". Here are the rules every model played by: Rule Why No thinking Every model answers directly. Mixing thinking and non-thinking models wouldn't be fair. One marked exception GPT-6 Astra can't switch thinking off, so the newest pair both think at "low". Marked ⚡ everywhere. Comparable pairs Each level pairs an Anthropic and an OpenAI model of the same class. Same prompts, same code English instructions, Georgian content, one task version for everyone. A fixed judge Translations are judged by Gemini 3 Flash, which isn't one of the tested models. Partial credit where it's fair Correction rewards every fixed error and penalizes every correct word broken. Failures never look like scores Above 5% failed calls, a task reports no score at all. Findings Drumroll, please. 🥁 Model Numbers Verbs Translation Cloze Correction Average Cost Claude Haiku 4.5 0.30 0.34 0.96 0.54 0.25 0.48 $0.10 GPT-5.4 mini 0.41 0.42 1.00 0.52 0.67 0.60 $0.05 Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.39 0.52 1.00 0.76 0.44 0.62 $0.29 GPT-5.4 0.46 0.54 1.00 0.88 0.66 0.71 $0.15 Claude Opus 4.8 0.54 0.68 1.00 0.84 0.68 0.75 $0.58 GPT-5.5 0.51 0.60 0.98 0.88 0.74 0.74 $0.30 Claude Opus 5 ⚡ 0.65 0.84 1.00 0.86 0.77 0.82 $1.22 GPT-6 Astra ⚡ 0.83 0.90 0.98 0.96 0.82 0.90 $1.73 Level by Level Light: GPT-5.4 mini beats Claude Haiku 4.5, 0.60 vs 0.48 , and costs half as much. Decent: GPT-5.4 beats Claude Sonnet 4.6, 0.71 vs 0.62 , again at about half the price. Top: Claude Opus 4.8 edges out GPT-5.5, 0.75 vs 0.74 . That's basically a tie. Newest ⚡: GPT-6 Astra beats Claude Opus 5, 0.90 vs 0.82 , the best score of the whole benchmark. It's ahead on four of the five tasks, with the biggest jump on numbers (0.83 vs 0.65). Final tally: OpenAI wins 3 of the 4 levels , and Anthropic's only win, at the top level, is basically a tie. One disclaimer: this is my dataset, my rules. Test other areas of Georgian and the results might shift a bit. That said, I tried to keep the tasks as broad and general as I could. Finding 1: Understanding Georgian Is Solved. Producing It Isn't. Look at the translation column: 0.96 to 1.00 for every model . Every one of them understands Georgian well enough to translate it into English almost perfectly. Now look at the other four columns. The moment a model has to produce correct Georgian (build a number, form a verb, inflect a word, fix a sentence), the scores drop hard. Without thinking, even the best model (Claude Opus 4.8) gets almost half of the number questions wrong. Only GPT-6 Astra, with its small thinking budget, gets above 0.80. Finding 2: Numbers Are the Final Boss Numbers are the hardest task for 6 of the 8 models, and close to the bottom for the other two. And inside it, the gap is wild: Question type Range across models Words → digits, cardinal 0.74 to 0.96 Words → digits, ordinal 0.04 to 0.92 Huge numbers, 10¹⁵ to 10³⁹ 0.06 to 0.53 Reading a Georgian number into digits: fine. Writing its ordinal in digits: disaster. GPT-6 Astra is the big exception there with 0.92, while the next best model gets 0.62. Remember მე-18 from earlier? Most models wrote the suffix form instead, because that's the pattern they've seen more often. With მე-40000 (forty-thousandth), only 2 of the 8 models got it right. Finding 3: The Mistakes Are Very Georgian My favorite part of the whole project is reading the wrong answers. They're not random. They're what you'd get if you tried to speak Georgian with grammar borrowed from somewhere else: "I fell in love with you." In Georgian, falling in love is an inversion verb: the one who loves is marked like an indirect object, so it's შემიყვარდი , literally "you became loved to me". Only GPT-6 Astra got it right. The others mostly built an ordinary transitive verb instead (შეგიყვარე). "We sat." Georgian uses a different verb root for sitting when the subject is plural: "I sat" is ვიჯექი, but "we sat" is ვისხედით . I planted ვიჯექით (a mix of the two) in a correction paragraph. Not a single model fixed it. "Who wrote it?" In დაგიწერია , the გ- marks "you" as the writer: "you have (apparently) written it". In the Georgian perfect, the markers flip. Only 2 of the 8 models got it right; the rest scattered across every other reading. One million. It's simply მილიონი . Most models write ერთი მილიონი ("one million") instead. Finding 4: Georgian Costs More Tokens for Claude Same prompts, same Georgian text, very different token counts. Claude models used 2 to 2.6 times more input tokens than GPT models for exactly the same questions: Task Claude, input tokens per call GPT, input tokens per call Numbers 272 104 Verbs 310 130 Cloze 1,412 699 Correction 404 159 Part of that is each vendor's answer-format instructions, and part is how each tokenizer splits Georgian script. In practice it means a Georgian prompt costs a Claude user noticeably more than the price per token suggests. Finding 5: Cheap Can Be Smart Cost per correct answer, on the tasks scored right or wrong: GPT-5.4 mini: 0.03 cents per correct answer. The bargain of the benchmark. Claude Opus 5 ⚡: 0.55 cents per correct answer, about 17 times the price of GPT-5.4 mini. GPT-6 Astra ⚡: 0.67 cents per correct answer. The best score, but about 21 times the price of GPT-5.4 mini per correct answer. Side Quest: The Uninvited Guest Remember Gemini 3.7 Flash, the model Kaggle runs automatically on every push? It's not part of my comparison, but it took the test every time I pushed, so I have its scores too. And it quietly scored around 0.89 on average , above every model in my table except GPT-6 Astra (0.90). The catch: even with thinking set to "none", it kept writing about 480 output tokens per number question , while the models without thinking wrote about 16. So it seems to keep thinking a little no matter what you tell it. Which leads to a fun takeaway: for a language like Georgian, thinking seems to matter more than model size . The two best models in my table, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, both think at "low" too. What It All Cost The whole project ran on Kaggle's free daily credits. Total spend across all the testing, probing and final runs: Cost Final comparison runs $4.63 Kaggle's automatic push runs $2.88 Earlier runs and cost probes $2.86 Local test runs $3.46 Total $13.84 Yes, the automatic push runs alone cost more than half as much as the actual benchmark. And spreading it over several days was the only way to stay under $10 a day. The Dashboard Tables are nice, but I wanted something you can actually explore. So all the results live on an interactive dashboard: Overview: the level-by-level showdown, the task matrix and the key findings Cost & tokens: what each model paid per task, the token gap, cost per correct answer and the full project spend Tasks: numbers by question type, verbs by type, correction split into fixed / missed / broken, and every cloze gap for every model Examples: real questions with every model's actual answer and an explanation of the mistake Method: where the data comes from, how each task is scored, the conditions and the limits It's a single static HTML page with no framework, no build step and no chart library, generated by a Python script straight from Kaggle's run files. So the dashboard and this article can never disagree. 👉 georgekobaidze.github.io/georgian-language-benchmarks Limitations Let's be honest about what this benchmark can and can't tell you: Hard by design. The sets keep mostly items a model got wrong, so the absolute scores are lower than they'd be on an easy set. The ranking is the meaningful part. Small sets. Some tasks have only 12 to 17 items, so a difference of a few points isn't significant. One run per model. Re-runs of the same model differed by about ±0.03 per task. The judge is a model. Translation scores depend on Gemini 3 Flash's judgment of meaning. The token gap includes format overhead , not only the tokenizer. What's Next Bigger sets. The full, untrimmed datasets are already in the repo's archive/ folder, ready for a run without the daily cap. More vendors. Google, xAI and the open models, once the budget allows. Thinking vs no thinking. The Gemini side quest begs for a proper experiment: the same model with and without thinking, on the same items. More Georgian. Native speakers are very welcome to contribute new items, corrections and alternative answers. My Benchmark 📊 Dashboard: georgekobaidze.github.io/georgian-language-benchmarks 🏆 Benchmark on Kaggle: kaggle.com/benchmarks/georgekobaidze/georgian-language-benchmark (the leaderboard only shows the models that ran on the latest version of the tasks, where the newest pair ran with "low" thinking; all 8 models are on the dashboard) 💻 Code: github.com/georgekobaidze/georgian-language-benchmarks Wrapping Up I started this with patches on one eye, and ended it with a benchmark, a dashboard and a lot of respect for how hard my own language is. The models understand Georgian almost perfectly. Producing it correctly is a whole different story, and that's exactly the gap this benchmark measures. And where the hell is my PhD? I've seen people (multiple of them) getting PhDs for exponentially less, and I'm not even kidding. I'm dead serious. If you speak Georgian, go check the Examples tab and tell me which mistake made you laugh the most. And if you have a good pirate nickname for me, you know where the comments are. If you don't speak Georgian and are planning to learn it, think twice and ask yourself if you're fully committed, because it can take a good 3 to 4 years (or more) of absolutely intense learning, and even then you'll be barely average. You are hunting an intermittent race condition, an elusive memory leak, or a broken build pipeline. Your eyes are dry and stinging from the 120Hz monitor. Your shoulders are hunched toward the keyboard. You re-read the exact same stack trace for the fourteenth time, convinced that if you just squint a little harder at line 142, the missing semicolon or dangling pointer will magically reveal itself. It never does. Instead, something biologically destructive is occurring inside your skull: Prefrontal Cortex Working Memory Exhaustion . In neuroscience, conscious analytical debugging relies strictly on the brain's Focused Mode —a high-energy neural state mediated by the prefrontal cortex and sustained by dopamine reserves. When you stay locked in focused mode for hours without reprieve, two cognitive breakdowns occur: Cognitive Tunneling (Einstellung Effect) : Your neural firing loops become rigid. The brain hyper-focuses on flawed initial assumptions, physically blinding you to lateral architectural solutions that are obvious in hindsight. Scotopic Ciliary Spasm : Staring at high-contrast pixels 50 centimeters from your face locks your eye lenses into continuous ciliary contraction, signaling persistent low-grade sympathetic stress to the central nervous system. The Screen-Locked Engineer The Natural Diffuse Reset Hours staring at the same stack trace Prefrontal cortex rests; Default Mode Network (DMN) engages Repeatedly running failed tests with no insight Associative memory connects non-adjacent conceptual nodes Ciliary eye strain from 50cm screen focus Distant optical horizon gazing relaxes lens muscles Dopamine depletion & irritable burnout Natural daylight exposure resets circadian rhythm and cortisol The great breakthroughs in computer science—from Archimedes stepping into the bath to developers realizing the solution to an architectural bug while stepping away from their desk—almost never happen while furiously typing. They happen when the conscious mind steps back and allows the Diffuse Mode (Default Mode Network) to subconsciously synthesize associative solutions across disparate memory networks. When DEV announced the Touch Grass Challenge for Week 1 of Hacktoberfest 2026 with the mandate: "Make the screen the shortest part of the experience." I knew I didn't want to build a gamified habit-tracker or another screen-heavy social dashboard that forces developers to look at their phone while outdoors. I built the exact opposite: an anti-distraction cognitive dispatcher designed to require under 15 seconds of screen interaction before closing your laptop, stepping outside into natural daylight, and letting diffuse biology solve the bug. I call it BreakPoint ☀️ . What I Built BreakPoint translates the core debugging principle of a software breakpoint— temporarily suspending execution to inspect state before resuming —into human biological hardware. It is an offline-first, client-side progressive web application that dispenses customized 15-, 20-, or 30-minute outdoor cognitive reset missions tailored to your specific mental blocker. BreakPoint Master UI System: Discharging digital work to step outside into natural daylight and diffuse thinking. What does it do, and how does it get people off the screen? Most wellness apps demand continuous attention with feeds, notifications, and gamification badges. BreakPoint is architected around the opposite principle: Zero-Screen Field Protocol . 15 Seconds Before Departure : Open BreakPoint, select your active fatigue blocker ( Complex Bug , Merge Conflict , Memory Leak , or Deploy Burnout ), pick a duration tier (15, 20, or 30 minutes), and get your solar trajectory. Zero Screens Moving : Pop in an earbud for a 20-second Web Audio acoustic briefing (432 Hz sine chime + spoken milestones) or glance at a 1080×1920 mobile lockscreen field card. Laptop Closed, Phone in Pocket : Step out the door. The app calculates your exact half-way turnaround time and observation milestones so you never have to unlock your screen during the walk. Stepping Away from the Screen As developers, we pride ourselves on persistence. We treat marathon debugging sessions as badges of honor, convincing ourselves that brute force and another cup of black coffee will eventually conquer the bug. Yet the biological reality is that software engineering is an act of creative synthesis, not mechanical data entry. When our prefrontal cortex is exhausted, more screen time only generates more friction, more bugs, and deeper cognitive fatigue. Building BreakPoint taught me that the most powerful debugging tool is often not another profiler, another breakpoint, or another AI chat window. It is the simple, humble decision to close the laptop lid, step outside into natural daylight, feel the sun on your face, and let your brain's diffuse mode do what millions of years of human biology evolved it to do.
